summary: The article examines the legal implications of prolonged Internet Service Disruptions (ISDs) following a 72-hour blackout beginning September 12, 2023, and later outages. It covers ISP contractual obligations under SLAs, consumer protection, regulatory and legislative responses, business impacts, international human rights, and steps individuals and businesses can take to protect their legal interests.
one_line: Overview of the legal consequences of prolonged internet outages after September 2023, covering SLAs, consumer rights, regulation, business risk, and protective strategies.
key_facts: A 72-hour internet blackout beginning September 12, 2023 affected millions of users across several states and prompted a nationwide discussion about legal ramifications.
On October 6, 2023, over 3 million users in a major metropolitan area lost service, reportedly due to aging infrastructure and cyberattacks.
On November 15, 2023, a rogue software update by ZYX Networks cut off users in three states for nearly 48 hours.
A class-action lawsuit was filed on December 5, 2023 against ZYX Networks for lack of transparency and inadequate compensation.
ISPs like ZYX Networks have contractual obligations in Service Level Agreements (SLAs), which often include uptime guarantees and compensation clauses.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) proposed new regulations to make ISPs more accountable for disruptions and improve communication with consumers during outages.
The California Internet Consumer Protection and Net Neutrality Act of 2024 provides a legal basis for compensation in the event of ISDs and mandates service quality and fair access.
Many insurers exclude ISDs from business interruption insurance policies; Roberta Anderson recommends cyber insurance and contingency plans.
Under international law, deliberate government internet shutdowns can be deemed violations of freedom of expression and press, per David Reynolds.
Following the November 20, 2023 nationwide blackout, collective actions compelled ISPs to settle disputes and offer compensation.
A National Internet Resilience Authority (NIRA) has been proposed to oversee efforts to strengthen internet infrastructure and response mechanisms.
Recommended protective steps include reviewing contracts, documenting communication with ISPs during disruptions, and joining class-action suits.
